title: Solaris remakes (1968, 1972, 2002) and could someone make a 'perfect' adaptation of it?

commenti.body: [removed]

Very interesting post!  The 1972 is definitely my favorite, a perfect film for Tarkovsky to make. But a Denis Villeneuve take on the novel would sertently be interesting! But I dont think anyone wants to make an other remake, not at  least for a long time..

I agree with the view that each movie misses the point by not dwelling sufficiently on the issue of otherness and how it cannot be subsumed within our conceptions of the same. The environment of Solaris forces humans to the realization that they do not know who or what they are, and that they themselves, too, are wholly other. In this regard, Solaris is a meta-commentary on science-fiction narratives: it's s veiled critique of sci-fi's genre tropes; since, if sci-fi is supposed to truly open out onto the irreducibly bizarre nature of things, why are we unable to break free of hoary narrative modes like heroic adventurers, domestic romance, imperialist expansion, etc.? These are all ways in which we anthropomorphize the Other, projecting onto the cosmos our own self-image. In that sense, it's a fascinating task and a paradoxical one: to create an image untethered by any preconceptions. I would like to see an animated adaptation. Films like Spirited Away have so much more freedom and artistic license.

Oh this just made something click in my mind that didn't before, it *could* in fact work so beautifully in animation, something similar to Magnetic Rose has the potential to embody that very well. Appreciate the thoughtful response!

It is funny because I ended up listening to the audiobook and I found it insufferable. It was cold and had little to offer beyond a few vaguely interesting science fiction what ifs. 

Also the ending of the book was just poor, and Tarkovsky’s ending understands the ideas of this ‘brain’ world so much better than the original author did. It reminds me of King/Kubrick and ‘The Shining’. Just like Kubrick Tarkovsky adds humanity, depth and beauty where there was little before. 

I totally understand why the author didn’t like the film, it simply wasn’t for him. It was an introspection on a single human life, the protagonist Kris Kelvin. It is humanistic not scientific. Where as the book is more generally just a pretty generic scifi tale and was written during a time when there was a glut of intentionally emotionless and hard science heavy ideas. The book would be unheard outside of heavy scifi fanbases if it wasn’t for Tarkovsky and maybe that’s what really grinds the authors gears, same with King. 

The way Tarkovsky brings Kris and hari alive in the film is unbelievable, I personally think it’s one of the most intense and emotional on screen relationships. Watching Kris desperately trying to hold onto this hallucinated Hari was tragic and felt very meaningful in terms of the human desire to be nostalgic over long lost loves. 

I watched the film for the first time only a bit after my first relationship break up. So that might explain why I’m so obsessed and defensive about it. 

The Soderbergh version…. Ughhhhh. 

I can’t stand Soderbergh, and I hate his way of basically re-using his favourite material and putting his little shine on things so he can make them his own. He made a half arsed film about Franz Kafka that is a similar type of flop as his version of Solaris, though Kafka is technically an original story. 

But really he is creating a mediocre collage and homage of much better material. As such his work can never and does never step out from the much greater original works. He can’t properly interpret or copy Kafka and neither can he Tarkovsky. And yes that is what he is desperately trying to do, he wants their importance and meaning but with his own little trademark squiggled over it. 

And for Solaris we get an apathetic and cringeworthy attempt to modernise the story. He actually follows the original book more so in parts, which only shows how the book as well as this film is wholly inferior to Tarkovsky’s. 

The emptiness that the Kris/Hari relationship has leaves the entire film feeling pointless and cold. Soderbergh either doesn’t understand Tarkovsky’s emotive humanism or is so incompetent he can’t even begin to touch it. 

I don’t recall enjoying the film at any point, and only finished it so I could be 100% certain it was garbage. But again biased because I can’t stand Soderbergh and quite literally have disliked everything I have seen of him.

I agree entirely on Soderbergh, I tried being diplomatic in my main post but HOW do you make a 100 minute long movie more of a bore than Tarkovsky's 3 hour one. 

And I was actually thinking very similar things about the vision of The Shining from King vs Kubrick. I couldn't stand the book but absolutely love how much Kubrick both added to, and trimmed from it.

I understand why Lem would be unhappy with Tarkovsky's vision since, well, it isn't *his* and they're two different creators. Tarkovsky has so much introspection and gentle insight on human nature that any adapted work becomes just a vessel of his own vision. Lem also hated Tarkovsky's adaptation of Roadside Picnic haha.

I will counter that from my perspective, I knew who Lem was and was familiar with his work before I even knew of Tarkovsky's existence - but my point of view is from an ex USSR country (he was more known here) and a family of sci-fi lit lovers. 

This one is obviously just up to personal preference, but gosh do I love some cold and dry 20th century sci-fi :D

I think in no way does Nolan or Villeneuve do a good job with the source material. 

You’d have to give it to a smaller director I think where they actually require creativity because of lack of budget. Those 2 have all the money in the world and still can’t make an engaging film.

That's a fair opinion! Some of the best sci-fi movies I know came from tight budgets, hell, look at Primer sitting at 7k. I personally am a fan of both the guys' work but I can understand how their stuff wouldn't be up everyone's alley. Something about colder, analytical sci-fi just speaks to me. I will agree that both Dune and Tenet were my least favourites of theirs, and both notably their biggest or one of the biggest budgets they got.. My personality flaw is that I loooove a grandiose expensive CG visual if done well, hence those two being my first thought :D

Well yeah you are in a very unique position to be very aware of Lem. 

Also I will say that probably the biggest criticism of Tarkovsky’s version is that 15 minute driving montage. It was all footage from Tokyo highways and he just liked the footage and wanted to use it. 

I will skip the entire sequence, in fact the whole Burton/naked baby thing most times. I just find it drags in just a bit too much. 

Though that being said the fact that this government meeting isn’t in the book shows you Tarkovsky directly referencing Kubrick and 2001. The meeting is reminiscent of the beginning of 2001 with Dr Floyd going to his interview and meetings. And Burton represents the experiences of the astronauts in the second half. 

And think the entire point of the Burton ‘commission’ is to mock that type of cold and emotionless sci fi of Lem and Kubrick in 2001. 

Also note that when Burton is describing what he saw from his craft he is quite literally describing the space baby from 2001. Burton doesn’t even exist in the book IIRC. This entire section is basically Tarkovsky dissecting and critiquing 2001 IMO. As well as comparing it’s cold and calculated approach to the Soviet’s own similar way of thinking about science and space. 

I love how much freedom and control Tarkovsky has to really show us through his world. I always think that one of the reasons you don’t see these types of films anymore is because directors can’t control their films as strongly as a Tarkovsky or Kubrick used to. Might be better for the mental health of the actors and set workers but not for the audience.

I actually kind of like the driving sequence (just like the 10 minute long star gate sequence from 2001) because I love it when directors will force their audience to engage with something like that, it's hilarious and anti hmmm art commodification to me?.. somehow? And knowing that today a big budget big name movie wouldn't even be allowed to do that because oh goodness gracious just think of those poor shareholders and the precious test screenings!

And yeah totally!! It's amusing to me how Tarkovsky was critical of how soulless 2001 was, while I personally adore both just for very different reasons. There's a place for everything, and if it wasn't for one the other may never have happened! It's lovely to see the flow and movement of art and artists and ideas.

I haven’t read the novel, but based on what you describe, I think Jonathan Glazer would do a fantastic job. Particularly with depicting the sense of dread and of otherness. I disagree with Nolan, as Interestelar can be very sentimental and melodramatic at times.

>The book would be unheard outside of heavy scifi fanbases if it wasn’t for Tarkovsky and maybe that’s what really grinds the authors gears, same with King.

Lem was very popular author in Soviet bloc. Just like op said before before Tarkovsky's film there was another USRR adaptation of Solaris. But Lem was not from USRR and he didn't write in Russian. His novels also started to be adapted since 50s despite being definitely challenging as scifi is not cheap. Tarkovsky's film made him and his book definitely more famous outside Soviet bloc because it comes out at the time of détente what made easier to him to be published on the west. Still obviously translations were so-so as Polish is not extremely popular language among translators. Actually real English translation come out like 10 years ago before that book was translated to English from French. Well the same problem is with Witcher which just has terrible English translation. 

Well definitely at least in Poland Lem's literature is much more popular than Tarkovsky as generally Poles taught themselves for ages to ignore Russian culture at least to the level which was possible. Of course a film was popular during communism but among younger generation unexpectedly watched it mostly people interested in cinema.
Ohh that's a good point! I've only ever seen Under the Skin from him but the whole experience is so deeply unsettling and strange that he would be a great fit for it!

Burton exists in the book.  Kelvin reads a transcript of his interview with the commission of enquiry in which the pilot recounts seeing the ocean form gardens and a giant toddler that moved in unnatural ways.

From what I know Lem and Tarkovsky didn't see eye to eye on a number of the director's ideas/decisions. As for your question I have two brief thoughts -- better to do a sit down over a glass of wine or two on this one. First I really liked the movie better than the book. The book's pacing didn't quite fit what I was hoping would exist. Secondly, we'd have to perhaps rule out books written after/about the movie such as 2001, which is what *that* book sucks so much. So ruling out those sorts of books might be useful. I thought Village of the Damned captured Wyndham's book quite well. Imagine now what Lav Diaz or Bela Tarr might do with Solaris. It could be both strange and wow.
Agreed I found the Soderbergh absolutely unwatchable garbage that lost anything important in the book in the service of a sped up plot for a larger low level consuming audience.

>It reminds me of King/Kubrick and ‘The Shining’. Just like Kubrick Tarkovsky adds humanity, depth and beauty where there was little before.

I can't disagree with this statement enough. Kubrick removed all of Jack's background and his struggles with alcoholism, anger issues, generational trauma, self doubt, projected self loathing, and genuine love for his family in the face of all that. He replaced it with an isolated crazy man who turns on his family because he's bored and ghosts feed him booze.
The second option sounds like the better movie to be honest.

> his main idea was to explore a situation where space exploration would attempt first contact only to fail at it because of the alien's absolute Otherness.

I think that's a concept almost impossible to film.  Its basically just something you write as a fact and if its true you can't and shouldn't be able, to do anything more with it.  Its like in writing when somebody says a monster is indescribably horrific, but then tries to describe the horror; it always fails. Either it can be described or it can't, so which is it?  

 I think the movie Annihilation attempted to do something like this in its final scenes.   And my impression is most people didn't know what the hell was going on and just thought it was weird, and wished it was more like the first 2/3rds of the movie.

> Kubrick removed all of Jack's background and his struggles with alcoholism, anger issues, generational trauma, self doubt, projected self loathing, and genuine love for his family in the face of all that. He replaced it with an isolated crazy man who turns on his family because he's bored and ghosts feed him booze.

And that choice was for the better.  The 97 mini series was true to the book, and it was definitely not the better film.

I never said the film would be better if it were a faithful adaptation. What I disagreed with was the statement that the film had more "humanity, depth and beauty" than the book. It objectively has less humanity and depth of character. Beauty is subjective and a meaningless comparison between different mediums.

> I never said the film would be better if it were a faithful adaptation.

I didn't say you did.  I said it was a better film for not including those elements.

> What I disagreed with was the statement that the film had more "humanity, depth and beauty" than the book. It objectively has less humanity and depth of character.

I agree, but like I said, it made for a better story not include those elements.

I don't think a perfect version of the movie could be done, or at least while still being something that would be successful as a movie in any way other than a visual spectacle. So much of the researchers' reactions to the ocean was in their heads and was beyond explanation. 

That being said, I like Tarkovsky's version best.

Also I think the ocean's otherness was most conveyed to me by the return of the protagonist's wife. She was so perfect a copy that she knew she shouldn't be there. Something that could create a copy of you so perfect that it \*was\* you? Spooky.

> Well yeah you are in a very unique position to be very aware of Lem.

I had read about a dozen Lem books before I knew who Tarkovsky was. I found out about Tarkovsky because I was describing Solaris to a guy in college and he said it sounded like that Tarkovsky movie. It was a lot easier to find Lem in bookstores than it was to see Soviet Film in the US in the 1980s. When my friend got and showed a print of Come and See that year, it was a big deal. Solaris did come to our local art house a year or two later though.

>I disagree with Nolan, as Interestelar can be very sentimental and melodramatic at times

That's because it was originally a Spielberg project that he passed on. The film is really Nolan trying his hand outside of what he's known for and pushing himself.

> Also I will say that probably the biggest criticism of Tarkovsky’s version is that 15 minute driving montage. It was all footage from Tokyo highways and he just liked the footage and wanted to use it. 

Wow, it goes for 15 minutes? Personally, I love that part of the movie and think it's beautiful, but if it actually goes for 15 minutes I could see that being too much for some people. I would have guessed 8 minutes at most.
I'm right there with you. I think the driving scenes are beautiful and would not change them.

I love love love the novel because (among a trillion other reasons) the metaphors and the images he creates with his language blend into each other a lot. At times it's unclear if he describes something relating to a deeper, philosophical aspect of what's going on or a literal thing that's happening, just using a very impressionistic language. It's so free that both could be meant at the same time. That psychedelic sense of drifting into another realm of reality (or our plane of existence losing importance) has not yet been translated into film adequately.

To me that's even the key to the ambiguous ending when he >!"gets carried away by the faceless colossus like a chip of wood"!< or something along the lines. >!It's unclear whether it's his physical self or his consciousness. It really doesn't matter anymore.!<

I was about to say it "cannot be done" but hey, maybe there's a film maker out there who could do it. I can only compare it to the really weird stuff out there - "Upstream Color" has a uniquely strange vibe to it that reminds me of that a bit. You don't get what's going on "cognitively" but if you just let go you will "feel" it correctly. I watched the film and basically had to read up on what the hell that was I just watched. But as it turned out all that was literally meant as I experienced it. Great film!

By the way, apparently that book has stayed very niche for a long time (still) because the English translation sucks. I can really imagine that all that doesn't work if a translator does not pay attention to his wording.

>...with a feeling of cosmic horror to it.

It's been a long time since I read the book, but in recollection this seems like entirely the wrong tone for the film as a whole.  Maybe in some brief instances.

> But I can imagine a more philosophical one with thriller elements, similar to the movie Sunshine.

That seems more like Lem to me.

Sure,  Blade Runner 2049, Arrival and Sicario are not engaging films at all.. what?
If anything, Arrival is quite successful at portraying the otherness of alien life forms.

The only one that felt unique in any way was Arrival. Blade runner was about half an hour too long and 2 hours over explained. Sicario was a trash heap of a movie with the single most annoying protagonist of all time. Over hyped garbage.
The horror part was probably just me being an impressionable teen haha! I might need to re-read it now with a fresh outlook
Disagree on all points except Arrival being unique.

On the basis of your post I watched Solyaris 1968 tonight. Quite interesting in comparison. I hadn't know about this before this and glad you brought it up. It would be a nice over a beer chat to discuss the two versions (I'm skipping that really shitty Soderbergh version that doesn't deserve comment). I felt in the first, the tight filming and pacing were very different and affected the idea of the whole. And I felt that the idea of an inability to understand the unknown was defeated in part by the scientistic approach and conclusion. But hey, so what, it was still fascinating to watch and thanks again.

I'm glad you enjoyed it!! Hilariously I started doing this little post writeup after I watched the 2002 one but then found out the 68 one exists on Letterboxd and was like Well Shit now I simply have to see this one before I can say anything productive on the topic

Eh, when Nolan came onto the project he rewrote a good bit of his brother's original script to suit his vision. And I wouldn't say *Interstellar* is really all that much more sentimental than *Inception* is in theory, just that *Interstellar* is a bit more blunt on that end (and less successful imo).
